title: The limits of consent
subtitle: Power, sex, and agency
author: Melissa Rees
introduction: Consent is of central importance in many areas of our lives, from sex to healthcare. But, argue Melissa Rees and Jonathan Ichikawa, consent should not become the only thing we care about in our relations with others. Many wrongdoings involving power imbalances resist explanation in terms of consent, and wrongs can take place even when consent is present. We must avoid seeing consent as the only ethical concept that matters in sexual relations and other areas of life. Consent matters, but it is not the only thing that matters.
body:
There are some things that, as we all know, you shouldn’t do without consent. Sex is one obvious example, but the role of consent in ensuring proper respect for people’s agency is central to moral conduct much more generally. For example, you can’t just take someone’s property. If you do, it’s theft. But if you ask for it and they give it to you—if they consent to your taking it—that’s a very different story.

Consent can “transform” an act that would otherwise have been violative into something welcome and respectful.

Or think about tattoos. In the ordinary course of life, you’re not allowed to stick needles into people and insert permanent ink in their skin. That’d be a serious physical assault. But if the tattoo happens with consent, it’s not assault, it’s a valued service. Heidi Hurd calls this the “moral magic” of consent. Consent can “transform” an act that would otherwise have been violative into something welcome and respectful.

Recognizing the presence or absence of consent is sometimes a simple matter. If someone is struggling against their bindings and screaming to be let go during the tattoo, they haven’t consented! If they made an appointment, explained what they wanted, and signed a waiver, that certainly looks like consent. But it doesn’t take too much imagination to see that sometimes there are subtler and less obvious factors that influence consent.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The politics of desire With Barry C. Smith, Zoe Strimpel, Maya Oppenheim, Kimberly McIntosh

Reputable tattoo shops won’t tattoo people who are intoxicated, and for good reason. If someone stumbles into a tattoo shop blackout drunk and asks for a tattoo, there’s a good case to be made that this is not genuine consent. Consent is an expression of agency; it requires a degree of competence and autonomy. Someone who is blackout drunk is not a full agent.

Ignorance can also interfere with consent. If someone asks for a tattoo without realizing that tattoos involve needles penetrating their skin, or that the image that it creates is permanent, there may well be good reason to think that wasn’t real consent. To give real consent, capable of performing its moral magic, people must understand, at least to some sufficient degree, what they are consenting to.

Likewise, it’s widely agreed that if someone is coerced to agree to something under duress—as if someone threatens to kill you unless you permit them to tattoo something on your body—that agreement doesn’t seem like the morally important kind of consent. For an agent to consent, they must do so more freely.

So if someone says “yes,” that isn’t always enough for consent. It also matters whether they were sufficiently competent, whether they have sufficient understanding, and whether they were coerced. Consent is an expression of agency, and not everyone who agrees to something does so as a genuine agent. Giving them a tattoo under these circumstances would wrong them, even if they were literally asking for it.

These observations aren’t just about tattoos; they’re about consent in general, including sexual consent. In the same way one shouldn’t be subjected to a tattoo without consent, one should also not be subjected to sexual contact without consent. Nonconsensual sexual contact is sexual assault.

There are cases where one should refrain from sexual contact, even when there is consent.

But consent isn’t the only important ethical concept to consider. People can be harmed by things they consent to. If someone asks for a terrible tattoo — one, for instance, that the tattoo artist has excellent reason to think they would later regret, the artist should probably refuse. If the artist is the tattoo requester’s close friend, they probably even have an obligationnot to give the terrible tattoo, even if there is full, sober, uncoerced consent. Friends owe it to each other to look out for each other, and not to do foreseeable harm.

We think the same goes for sexual relationships. There are cases where one should refrain from sexual contact, even when there is consent. There are many unjust, unethical, harmful sex acts, or even whole sexual relationships, that are entirely consensual. This is especially common when it comes to sexual relationships with power imbalances (due to age gaps, for example, or between employers and employees, or teachers and students). We think a lot of contemporary discourse about such cases involves misapplying the notion of consent. Such relationships are often violative; people are sometimes tempted to explain this violation by saying that sexual relationships of these kinds are always nonconsensual. We think this violation should be explained in different terms. When consent is the only tool in one’s conceptual toolkit in sexual ethics, the wronged party can actually get exposed to further harms (we’ll focus on this a little later).

Why might power imbalances threaten consent? Could it be because they are coercive? No doubt, power imbalances sometimes give rise to clear cases of coerced, nonconsensual sex. But we don’t think this is the correct description of the less clear cases that are our focus. For coercion to undermine consent, it must amount to more than the ordinary ways people make choices guided by their (sometimes conflicting or amorphous) preferences, desires, and goals, as they navigate a complex social world with unjust social rewards and social sanctions. And at least some relationships of this kind do not feel coercive to the less powerful person. Is every such person wrong to say that they weren’t coerced? We don’t think so.

SUGGESTED VIEWING How to fix sexual assault law With Emma Bryson

Or might there be something about power imbalances that makes less powerful sex partners incompetent to consent? In some cases, perhaps. But we perceive a tendency to underestimate competence in these cases. We call this phenomenon agential demotion: when someone is indeed capable of consenting but is conceived as having agency so severely compromised that they are incapable of consenting. When someone isn’t capable of consenting, you aren’t agentially demoting them when you see them as such. Agential demotion is by definition a mistake–a special kind of error where we ‘demote’ someone from the status of agent to non-agent, from capable to incapable. We think part of the allure of agential demotion is to emphasize that the blame for the violation does not rest with the victim: to avoid victim-blaming, one might conceptualize the relationship entirely as something a perpetrator did to a hapless victim, whose behaviour did not amount to agential participation or consent. But as we’ll explain below, we don’t think agential demotion is a helpful way to achieve these goals.

Some people do lack the competence to consent, due to intoxication, or age, or other reasons. But we cannot accept that power imbalances always rob the less powerful person of their capacity to consent. In many cases, they do consent and they are wronged nevertheless. Reducing all sexual wrongdoing to one kind of violation—nonconsensuality—does a disservice to the person who has been wronged.

Conceiving of yourself as a severely compromised agent—so compromised that you lacked the very capacity to consent—can be harmful.

Imagine that a 16-year old is in a sexual relationship with a legal adult. Such relationships are widely seen as violative, even if both parties seem to consent. We agree! But we resist the idea that the wrong at hand is always due to incompetence to consent. The teenager may robustly expresses their agency in a wide variety of arenas; they understand consequences, they are informed, they confidently pursue what they want in life. If there is no deception or coercion, then it is hard to see how to motivate the idea that they are capable of consent to sexual activity with a teenage peer, but are not capable with a person who is older. The latter situation doesn’t have to be nonconsensual to be deeply wrong, deeply harmful*.* Importantly, feeling moral disgust at such a situation, making efforts to end that relationship, or condemning the older party for their moral wrongdoing, does not entitle us to agentially demote the teenager. If sexual wrongdoing is only ever determined by the presence or absence of consent, then victims of wrongs like these face a dilemma: either stay firm in their judgment that they consented and give up the idea that they were wronged, or stay firm in their judgment that they were wronged and agentially demote themselves—treating themselves as having lacked agency, and so, treating their agreement as morally unimportant.

Conceiving of yourself as a severely compromised agent—so compromised that you lacked the very capacity to consent—can be harmful. It amounts to a kind of objectification; one sees oneself less as a person acting in the world, and more as an object being acted upon. This can lead to feelings of worthlessness; it can also easily lead to increased self-doubt about future interactions. One wonders: “Is my agency compromised, even now?” That doubt itself can sometimes undermine genuine agency.

Besides these harms, we also don’t think agential demotion is likely to do a good job protecting victims of these kinds of relationships from blame. Regrettably, victim-blaming (both first-personally and third-personally) remains common even in sexual assaults where it is obvious that there was no consent. So, there is good reason to believe that agentially demoting someone is unlikely to protect them from blame or shame. We think the better solution is to recognize that that consent doesn’t guarantee the ethical good standing of sexual activity, and that agential demotion can itself be harmful.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The morality of sex With Myriam François, Steven Bonnell, Maya Oppenheim, Isabel Millar, Sophie Scott-Brown

We need to enrich our understanding of sexual ethics; not everything is about consent. Diagnosing how someone has been sexually wronged, even in the presence of their consent, must always be local, specific, and context sensitive. However, broad patterns do arise. We believe that people who hold more powerful social roles can owe special obligations to those who are less powerful—duties to protect their interests, safeguard their well-being, and promote their agency. And this is especially true when one has a close intimate relationship with someone, the way sex partners typically do with one another. (Recall the tattoo artist who has an obligation not to give their friend a terrible tattoo, even if they ask for it.)

Complicating this dynamic, sexual relationships can also obscure these asymmetries. We often feel like equals with our partners—which is not to say we are blithely unaware of the power imbalance when one party is at a social, educational, or economic disadvantage. Rather, the sexual relationship (and feeling of parity that comes with it) can make it harder to recognize that the more powerful incur stronger, stricter, or more binding obligations to refrain from action that is likely to cause harm or discomfort. This is an additional reason such relationships can be so morally fraught.

We’ve focused on sexual relationships between underage teenagers and adults, arguing that they often involve serious moral wrongs despite the presence of genuine consent. But this analysis, we think, extends further to many other kinds of power imbalances as well. Reflecting upon these cases, on their nuance and the discomfort they generate, can, we hope, improve moral understanding without sacrificing our regard for the agency of the people involved.
